In addition, ecological issues and technological progress affect the two age groups differently: younger adults report higher levels of eco-anxiety-a new form of distress caused by climate change disasters (Pihkala, 2020)-and greater concerns about ecological issues (APA, 2018; Hill-Harding et al., 2025), whereas older adults experience greater physical consequences of climate change due to their potential exacerbation of pre-existing health conditions (Ayalon et al., 2023). Similarly, younger adults, who typically engage more extensively in technology-based activities, appear to be at greater risk of problematic Internet use (Lozano-Blasco et al., 2022), whereas older adults report greater difficulties with technology acceptance and use (Adams et al., 2005; Harris et al., 2022; Fini et al., 2025). Such generational differences in experience, familiarity, and perceived relevance may, in turn, shape the properties considered most salient and the level of abstraction at which these concepts are represented. In this regard, two multi-task studies reveal that the level of abstractness in the representation of ecological (Falcinelli et al., 2025a) and technological (Falcinelli et al., 2024b) concepts varies in relation to age groups: ecological concepts were represented with more concrete properties by older adults (aged >65) as compared to younger adults (aged 18-35) (rating task); conversely, technological concepts were represented more concretely by younger adults, who also processed related words faster than older adults (categorization task). In addition, despite some similarities, the two age groups differed in the key features considered most salient for characterizing ecological and technological concepts (feature generation task).

Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts

To shed further light on age group differences in the representation of green and technological concepts, our study replicates and extends Falcinelli et al. (2024a). Our work is a replication, since the methodology is the same: we asked participants to evaluate the same set of concepts on the same semantic dimensions. As a novelty, here the sample is composed of older citizens (aged >64) rather than younger individuals. In order to detect differences across age groups in the conceptual representation of green and technological concepts, we compared the newly collected data on older adults with previously collected data on younger adults (aged 18-35) from Falcinelli et al. (2024a).

To this end, we employed a Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (Barker & Rayens, 2003; Nguyen & Rocke, 2002), which is an exploratory multivariate dimensionality-reduction technique widely used in metabolomics (e.g., Pérez-Enciso & Tenenhaus, 2003; Rohart et al., 2017; Worley, 2013; Worley et al., 2013), but that we applied for the first time to study semantic organization. This innovative use of PLS-DA enabled us I) to assess the similarity of conceptual representations of the different semantic domains within each age group; and II) to identify the semantic aspects that most strongly differentiate each age group within each conceptual domain, providing insights into the complexity (i.e., semantic richness and variety) and concreteness of their semantic representations across age groups.

So far, researchers interested in collecting evaluations on concepts' characteristics (i.e., semantic norms) have explored specific conceptual classes, i.e., abstract and concrete concepts (e.g., Brysbaert et al., 2014; Diveica et al., 2023) or sub-kinds of them (for overviews, see Borghi et al., 2018b; Conca et al., 2021; Villani et al., 2019). Data were usually collected on the general population regardless of age or mostly on younger individuals, and evaluations related to few dimensions usually taught to distinguish between abstract and concrete concepts (e.g., concept's abstractness, familiarity, imageability, and linking to contexts) and, in most cases, separately detected on different wordpools (e.g., Bennett et al., 2011; Brysbaert et al., 2014; Diveica et al., 2023; Lynott & Connell, 2013; Lynott et al., 2020; Tillotson et al., 2008; for Italian examples, see Della Rosa et al., 2010; De Varda et al., 2025; Montefinese et al., 2014; Repetto et al., 2023; Villani et al., 2019).

Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts

Our work aims to enrich this literature. First, we investigate domains, especially ecological and technological, that are quite relevant in the modern era and greatly impact people's lives. In addition, these domains have undergone many conceptual changes in recent years, making them ideal for studying conceptual change and for exploring differences and similarities across two age groupsolder and younger individuals. Second, their hybrid nature (Falcinelli et al., 2024a, b; Falcinelli et al., 2025a) makes their study challenging for theories of concepts assuming a concrete-abstract dichotomy.

Compared with previous work, our study explore the characterization of such domains by investigating multiple dimensions (N = 39) on the same word set related to various kinds of experiences, such as sensorimotor (e.g., activation of external experiences through body and senses), inner (e.g., activation of inner experiences such as interoception and mental processes), emotional (e.g., valence and emotional charge of a concept), metacognitive (e.g., confidence and need of outsourcing to understand/master a conceptual meaning) and sociopolitical (e.g., social and political relevance of a concept), along with aspects traditionally employed to distinguish between abstract and concrete concepts (e.g., level of abstractness, imageability and linkability to contexts of a conceptual referent). Based on this, our approach is in line with recent theories (i.e., Multiple Representation Views - Barsalou et al., 2018; Borghi, 2022 Borghi, , 2023;; Borghi et al., 2017; 2018a; Crutch et al., 2013; Dove, 2009 Dove, , 2014 Dove, , 2022;; Harpaintner et al., 2018; Kiefer & Harpaintner, 2020; Reilly et al., 2025; Troche et al., 2017; Villani et al., 2019; Zdrazilova et al., 2018) which propose to study concepts in a more complex way by conceiving them as points in a multidimensional space defined by multiple features, where concreteness~abstractness is just one of the possible dimensions of investigation, rather than simply rely on the classical concrete-abstract dichotomy or continuum (Borghi, 2023).

Finally, beyond its theoretical contributions, the present work also offers practical benefits: it extends the TECo database developed by Falcinelli et al. (2024a)-which provides normative data for ecological, geo, natural, and technological concepts, primarily collected from younger adults-by incorporating new ratings from older adults (the O-TECo database; see section 4 for details). To the Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts best of our knowledge, this is the first database to specifically offer semantic norms for an older adult population. In addition, along with the original database, it is also the first one covering a broad range of semantic dimensions across emerging conceptual domains, moving beyond the traditional distinction between abstract and concrete concepts.

1.1. Experimental Hypotheses

Our hypotheses concerned both between-domain comparisons and within-domain comparisons across age groups.

First, are semantic representations more similar across green (ecological, geo, and natural) domains than between green and technological domains within each age group? (between-domain comparison) We expected, for each age group, greater semantic similarity among green concepts (ecological, geo, and natural) than with technological concepts, as they share a common reference to the natural environment, albeit capturing different aspects: geo and natural concepts concern environmental entities and features, whereas ecological concepts emphasize the environmental consequences of human activities. Conversely, we expected technological concepts to show greater differentiation from the green domains for both older and younger adults, given their focus on technology-related entities and phenomena rather than on the natural environment.

Second, do older and younger adults differ in the complexity and concreteness of their semantic representations within each domain? (within-domain comparison) We expected age-group representations to vary in terms of their complexity-defined as the richness and variety of semantic aspects contributing to the organization of each domain-, and concreteness.

Specifically, based on previous evidence showing greater engagement in pro-environmental behaviors and nature-related activities among older than younger adults (e.g., Ágoston et al., 2024; López-Mosquera et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021), we hypothesized that older adults Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts would characterize green concepts in a richer and more multifarious way than younger adults-i.e., with a semantic representation that includes more dimensions and components (see section 3.2.2). Conversely, we expected younger adults to characterize technological concepts more elaborately than older adults, potentially reflecting their greater life experience with technology (for a review, see Hunsaker & Hargittai, 2018).

In addition, based on Falcinelli et al. (2024a), we expected all conceptual domains to exhibit a hybrid characterization, combining abstract-like and concrete-like features, with representations shifting towards greater concreteness in semantically richer and more varied domains due to stronger experiential grounding (Mazzuca et al., 2025; Villani et al., 2022). Accordingly, we hypothesized that older adults would show a more concrete representation of green concepts (Falcinelli et al., 2025a), whereas younger adults of technological concepts (Falcinelli et al., 2024b). More concrete representations would be characterized, for instance, by greater relevance of experiential and sensorimotor aspects, higher contextual availability and imageability, stronger interactions between the body and the referent, greater familiarity, and greater ease of definition and word mastery. Conversely, more abstract representations would be characterized by greater political and social relevance of the semantic domain, higher emotionality and interoceptive experience, greater reliance on others and experts to acquire an understanding of the concepts, and a greater perceived psychological distance from them.

2. Data Availability

Experimental materials, raw data, analysis scripts of the study, and the normative data on older adults (the O-TECo database) are available at the following OSF repository: https://osf.io/skr5p/?view_only=c120d4b410e747de8352fb086895125e. The study was not preregistered.

Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts >Methods >Participants

3.1.1 Older adults

We based the sample size on previous rating studies (Falcinelli et al., 2024a; see also Stadthagen-Gonzalez & Davis, 2006; Vankrunkelsven et al., 2024; Villani et al., 2019), which typically include around 20 participants per word and semantic dimension. This choice is also consistent with simulation-based evidence suggesting that approximately 10 ratings provide stable estimates, as confidence intervals tend to plateau before this threshold (Motamedi et al., 2019; see also Winter et al., 2024). Given that we administered 16 surveys (see section 3.3), a total sample of 320 participants was needed.

We collected data between March 23 rd , 2023, and June 3 rd , 2024. Participants volunteered to take part in the study without any compensation, and we recruited them through word-of-mouth or by sponsoring surveys on social media (i.e., Facebook). The inclusion criteria for the study were being Italian native speakers aged 64 or older. At first, we set the age threshold at 65 years, as this is commonly used in psychological research on older adults (e.g., Falcinelli et al., 2024b; Falcinelli et al., 2025a; Zaitchik & Solomon, 2008; Wulff et al., 2022). We then slightly decreased it because some participants aged 64 were also tested (n = 3), and we did not want to discard their data since they were of good quality (see exclusion criteria below). It is worth noting that the current age cutoff guidelines to define older adults are still controversial (Orimo et al., 2006), and some works put it lower (for example, Cain & Ryskin, 2025: 63 years old; Hess, 1982: 64 years old), so we can confidently include these participants in our study. We did not conduct specific screening for cognitive impairment or mild cognitive decline for older adults, as the task involved collecting explicit subjective judgments rather than assessing cognitive functioning through more implicit measures (e.g., reaction times).

A total of 1488 participants completed surveys, but we excluded 1094 of them because their compilations were incomplete, most of which were close to zero in terms of survey completion Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts progress, likely due to the length of the surveys (for a similar procedure, see Falcinelli et al., 2024a; see also Brysbaert et al., 2014). In addition, we discarded 6 participants under 64 years old and a further 56 participants because their data consistently lacked variability, thus qualifying as outliers (for a similar procedure, see Falcinelli et al., 2024a; see also Della Rosa et al., 2010). As an additional criterion for excluding outliers, we included four attention checks per dimension in the surveys and discarded participants who failed more than 2 attentional checks for each dimension (Falcinelli et al., 2024a). However, no participant failed to respond correctly to these items more than twice. Finally, we eliminated 18 participants who met all inclusion criteria (i.e., complete compilation, Italian native speakers aged over 64, not outliers) but exceeded the number of ratings needed for each survey (N = 20). We did so to have an equal and comparable number of compilations across questionnaires, faithfully replicating the procedure adopted by Falcinelli et al. (2024). In cases of over-compilation, we used a sample as old as possible, keeping the questionnaires filled out by the oldest participants.

Therefore, the final sample comprised 320 older Italian participants (231 females, M age = 70.71; SD age = 5.25; Range age = 64 -94). Their socio-demographic information can be found in Table S1, Supplementary Materials (from now on, "SM". SM can be downloaded from the OSF repository: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/SKR5P).

3.1.2 Compared samples of younger and older individuals

To compare data from older and younger adults, we first selected the data from each age group.

Ratings from older adults were collected specifically for the present study (see section 3.3.1), whereas ratings from younger adults were taken from Falcinelli et al. (2024a). Because the sample in Falcinelli et al. (2024a) was composed mostly, but not entirely, of younger adults, we first restricted the younger sample to evaluations provided by participants aged 35 or younger (in line with Falcinelli et al., 2024b; Falcinelli et al., 2025a). For the older group, we included participants aged 64 or above. We then matched the number of ratings contributing to each word per dimension across the two age groups. Although equal numbers of ratings are not a formal requirement of the subsequent analyses (PLS-DAs, see section 4), we adopted this procedure to ensure that the aggregated scores were based Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts on comparable amounts of data across groups, thereby reducing potential differences in the precision and reliability of the mean ratings. Specifically, we retained evaluations from the oldest participants in the present study until the number of ratings matched that of the younger group, thereby also maximizing the age gap between the two experimental groups. Detailed information on the resulting samples is provided in Table S2 (SM).

Thus, we performed comparisons between 236 older (168 females, M age = 71.99; SD age = 5.13, Range age = 64 -94) and 239 younger adults (162 females, M age = 25.67; SD age = 3.39, Range age = 18 -35)foot_0 . Details on their socio-demographic characteristics can be found in Table S3, SM.

To ensure that the subgroups of older and younger individuals evaluating the same dimension significantly differed in mean age, we fitted a linear model featuring age as a dependent variable and the interaction between Age Group (Older, Younger) and Dimension (N = 39) as a fixed factor. The model showed a significant interaction between Age Group and Dimension, F(38, 1082) = 5.94490, p < .0001, Cohen's d = 10.64, suggesting that each paired sub-group of older and younger individuals who provided ratings for the same dimension significantly differ in their age, with the older group representing the oldest one across all dimensions (all p s < .0001 -for details, see Table S4, SM). In addition, the mean ages of subgroups were quite similar within experimental groups across dimensions (see Table S2, SM).

3.2. Materials

>Materials

3.2.1. Words

The stimulus consisted of 200 Italian target words, classified into four categories: ecological, geo, natural, and technological concepts (n = 50 each, Falcinelli et al., 2024a). Ecological concepts included terms related to climate change phenomena (e.g., global warming, greenhouse effect, ozone hole) or to the factors that cause them (e.g., deforestation, industrial drain, intensive agriculture).

Natural concepts comprised words referring to natural entities like environmental elements (n = 12, e.g., atmosphere, oxygen, water), atmospheric events (n = 12, e.g., blaze, flood, thunderstorm), Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts animals (n = 13, e.g., bee, turtle, whale), and plants (n = 13, e.g., flower, olive tree, pine). Geo concepts included terms referring to natural (geographical, n = 25; e.g., desert, mountain, ocean) and urban entities or locations (geopolitical, n = 25; e.g., country, megalopolis, Western). Finally, technological concepts encompassed words unrelated to the green domain and referring instead to informatics and technology-i.e., mainly devices and software commonly used for online communication and interaction (e.g., cellphone, computer, Internet). The full set of words is available in Table S5, SM (for details on word selection and validation, see Falcinelli et al., 2024a).

3.2.2. Semantic Dimensions

Participants rated the complete list of words on 39 semantic dimensions (Falcinelli et al., 2024a). We divided these dimensions into distinct groups (henceforth, "components") based on previous literature examining their relevance to defining abstractness.

Abstractness component. This component includes dimensions that are typically investigated to address differences between abstract and concrete concepts. They are: Concreteness~Abstractness, which captures how concrete~abstract a concept is perceived to be (Paivio et al., 1988; Paivio, 1990; Villani et al., 2019); Imageability (Paivio et al., 1988; Paivio, 1990; Villani et al., 2019) and Context Availability (Schwanenflugel et al., 1992; Villani et al., 2019), referring, respectively, to how easily a concept evokes mental images and can be associated with contexts; Body-Object-Interaction, measuring how easy it is to physically interact with the object to which a concept refers (Bennett et al., 2011; Siakaluk et al., 2008; Tillotson et al., 2008; Villani et al., 2019); Familiarity, indicating the perceived level of knowledge of a concept (Barca et al., 2002); two measures related to word acquisition, i.e., Age of Acquisition (Gilhooly & Logie, 1980), referring to how early or late a concept is perceived to be learned, and Modality of Acquisition (Wauters et al., 2003), which concerns whether a concept is mainly acquired through sensorimotor or linguistic experiences; and Frequency (Laudanna & Burani, 1995), indicating the estimated frequency of use of a word in the written and spoken language. Along the aforementioned dimensions, this component also included a measure Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts referring to how easily participants feel they can define a concept (Easiness Of Providing a Definition -Falcinelli et al., 2024a).

Second, in line with suggestions of Multiple Representation Views (e.g., Borghi, 2023; Borghi & Binkofski, 2014; Borghi et al., 2018b; Diveica et al., 2025; Dove, 2009 Dove, , 2022;; Pexman et al., 2023), we included semantic dimensions testing to what extent concepts evoke different kinds of experiences.

Sensorimotor & Experiential component. This component targets sensorimotor experiences with Perceptual Strength, measuring the extent to which a conceptual referent can be experienced through the five sensory modalities-vision, touch, hearing, taste, and smell (Connell & Lynott, 2012 , 2014; Lynott & Connell, 2013; Villani et al., 2019); Action Effectors, assessing how strongly a concept is perceived to engage specific body parts, i.e., feet/legs, hands/arms, mouth/throat, and torso (Lynott et al., 2020); and Personal Experience, indicating the perceived extent to which a concept is experienced firsthand (Falcinelli et al., 2024a).

Emotional & Inner component. This component investigates inner and emotional experiences through Interoception, capturing the perceived degree to which a word evokes interoceptive bodily states (Connell et al., 2018; Villani et al., 2019 Villani et al., , 2021)); Metacognition, referring to the perceived extent to which a concept triggers mental or cognitive processes (Villani et al., 2019); Emotionality, assessing the amount of emotional content associated with a concept (Ponari et al., 2018; Vigliocco et al., 2014; Villani et al., 2019); and Valence, Dominance, and Arousal, that refer, respectively, to the emotional tone of a concept (negative~positive), the perceived level of control over its referent, and the degree of internal activation the word elicits (Montefinese et al., 2014).

Social Metacognition component.

This component targets socio-metacognitive aspects, including Word Confidence and Confidence in Experts (Mazzuca et al., 2022), which estimate how confidently individuals believe they master the meaning of a word and how confidently they think experts in the relevant field do so, respectively. We also included Other Social Metacognition, indicating the extent to which people feel they need to rely on others to grasp the meaning of a concept Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts (Borghi, 2022; Borghi et al., 2018a, b; Borghi et al., 2019a, b; Villani et al., 2019), and Expert Social Metacognition, which mirrors Other Social Metacognition, but specifies that individuals to rely on are the domain experts (Falcinelli et al., 2024a).

Sociopolitical component. This component includes Social Valence, measuring the extent to which a concept is perceived to evoke social situations (Falcinelli et al., 2024a; see also Diveica et al., 2023; Pexman et al., 2023; Villani et al., 2019), two dimensions related to pragmatic/communicative aspects-i.e., Easiness to Start a Conversation, reflecting how easily a concept can initiate a discussion, and Openness to Negotiation, indicating how willing people are to negotiate or discuss a concept's meaning with others (Fini et al., 2023), and Political Relevance, a measure capturing how a concept might spark public and societal debate (Falcinelli et al., 2024a; see also Mazzuca & Santarelli, 2023).

Impact component. This component includes dimensions related to the influence of a concept on people's lives-specifically, its perceived impact in their past, present, and future (Perceived Impact in the Past, Present, and Future - Falcinelli et al., 2024a) and the extent to which it is perceived psychologically closer or farther (Perceived Distance -Mazzuca et al., 2022).

Naturalness~Artificiality component. This component encompasses two dimensions, i.e., perceived Scientificity and Naturalness-Artificiality, assessing whether a conceptual referent is judged to belong more to natural objects or artifacts (Falcinelli et al., 2024a; see also Forde & Humphreys, 2005).

The operationalization of the dimensions and the Italian and English versions of the instructions are available in the OSF repository (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/SKR5P).

3.3. Procedure

Ethics permission was granted by the Ethics Committee of the Department of Dynamic and Clinical Psychology, and Health Studies, Sapienza University of Rome (Prot. n. 000147 -04/02/2022). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Participants took part in an Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts online survey on the Qualtrics platformfoot_1 . They compiled the questionnaire at home using a laptop, and if they were not accustomed to technology, an experimenter assisted them.

Before beginning the survey, participants were informed about the study's general aims and asked to provide informed consent for their participation and the publication of the results. After consenting, they proceeded with the rating task. Participants evaluated target words across the semantic dimensions using a 7-point Likert scale and were instructed to answer carefully yet efficiently, without overthinking each item. Each word was presented individually with a brief framing text followed by the relevant Likert scale. To ensure attentiveness, we embedded four attention checks per dimension, requiring participants to match a geometric figure to its corresponding name.

In the final part of the survey, participants provided socio-demographic information, i.e., age, birth sex, education level, employment status, socio-economic status, city and region of origin, whether Italian was their first language, and proficiency in an additional language. They also indicated whether their place of origin and current residence were rural or urban and rated their perceived level of expertise on green topics using a 7-point Likert scale (see Table S1, SM) (for a similar procedure, see Falcinelli et al., 2024a). The survey's compilation took an average of 1.5 hours per participant. We allowed participants to pause the experiment at any time and restart it at their own pace as long as they handed in the survey within two weeks from the start-a more flexible deadline than the 72 hours used in Falcinelli et al. (2024a), to minimize dropout, considering the questionnaires' length and the sample's age.

We administered 16 surveys, each compiled by an independent pool of 20 participants. Participants rated the full set of words on two semantic dimensions within each survey, resulting in an average of 400 trials per survey (i.e., 200 words rated on two dimensions) (Falcinelli et al., 2024a; see also Villani et al., 2019). Just a few surveys (n = 3) included more than two dimensions because they represented subaspects of the same "broader" dimension (e.g., Past, Present, and Future within "Perceived Impact"). The survey structure is available in the OSF repository (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/SKR5P).

Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts

4. Data Analysis

Data was pre-processed and analyzed through R (R Core Team, 2023) and RStudio (version 4.5.0).

The "Tidyverse" R package (Wickham et al., 2019) was used to handle data and prepare datasets for analyses. Figure 1 provides a schematic overview of the analytical approach undertaken in the present study.

Older adults' data cleaning, descriptive statistics, and the O-TECo database (see Figure 1, point 1). In line with our exclusion criteria (see section 3.1), we discarded 78.50% of older adults' data. The final dataset was therefore composed of 156,000 data points, with 20 ratings per word and per dimension. As a first step, we estimated the internal consistency of ratings from each pool of 20 participants for each dimension, expressed as Cronbach's alpha (Cronbach, 1951; see Falcinelli et al., 2024a). Cronbach's alphas were excellent for all dimensions (M = 0.98; SD = 0.01), ranging from 0.96 to 1.00 (see Table S6, SM). We also assessed inter-rater reliability, calculating a two-way random-effects, absolute-agreement, average-measures intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC[2,k]; Shrout & Fleiss, 1979; Koo & Li, 2016), treating participants as raters and target words as targets.

The ICC was good for all dimensions (M = 0.82; SD = 0.12), ranging from 0.46 to 0.99 (see Table S6, SM).

As a second step, we calculated summary statistics per dimension (median, mean, standard deviation, standard error, range, and the words with the highest and lowest scores; see Table S7, SM). Finally, by calculating the mean and standard deviation for each target word across each dimension, we created the O-TECo database (Older adults-Technological and Ecological Concepts database), containing semantic norms tailored to older adults for ecological, geo, natural, and technological concepts. Along with our 39 targeted dimensions (see section 3.2.2), the O-TECo database also includes information on words' objective frequency score and on their length and number of syllables Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts (Falcinelli et al., 2024a). The database is publicly available at the OSF repository (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/SKR5P).

Characteristics of the compared samples of older and younger individuals (see Figure 1, point 2). To better characterize the selected samples of older and younger adults (see section 3.1.2), we explored whether there were differences between the two generations in familiarity and personal experiences with the four conceptual domains, as well as in their perceived level of expertise in green topics (see section 3.3). Indeed, such factors, along with age, may be important in shaping conceptual representations (e.g., Mazzuca et al., 2025; Villani et al., 2022). To this end, we first considered data on familiarity and personal experiences (see section 3.2.2) and ran two separate ordinal regression mixed models using the "ordinal" R package (Christensen, 2022). The models featured ratings on the dimension of interest as a dependent variable, the interaction between Age Group (Older, Younger) and Category of Word (Ecological, Geo, Natural, Technological) as a fixed factor, and Target Word and Participants as random intercepts. We determined the significance of the interactions through Type III ANOVAs. Then, we assessed differences in green expertise across age groups by fitting an ordinal regression model with such ratings as the dependent variable and Age Group (Older, Younger) as a fixed factor. The significance of the main effect was determined through a Type II ANOVA.

PLS-DAs to examine between-and within-domain semantic differences across age groups (see Figure 1, point 3).

To explore differences between older and younger adults in their conceptual representations across and within semantic domains, we performed four separate multilevel Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analyses (PLS-DAs) on ratings provided by the two age groups to ecological, geo, natural, and technological concepts. PLS-DA is a partial least squares regression of a group of binary variables delineating the categories of a categorical variable on a collection of predictor variables (Pérez-Enciso & Tenenhaus, 2003). This technique has been widely used over the past two decades in the field of metabolomics (Barker & Rayens, 2003; Nguyen & Rocke, 2002; Rohart et al., 2017; Worley, 2013; Worley et al., 2013), and can be thought of as a "supervised" version of Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Indeed, similarly to PCA, it transforms a dataset with many observations and a large number of features (in our case, semantic dimensions) into a smaller one composed of latent components (Principal Components -PCs) that still contain as much variance of the original dataset as possible, but differently from PCA, it considers the class to which observations belong (in our case, target words by older and younger adults), thus allowing for between-groups discrimination (Botella et al., 2009; Christin et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2004). Latent components are linear combinations of the original semantic dimensions, and the first one (from now on, "PC1") captures the main axis that best discriminates between targeted groups, such that observations (in our case, target words) are positioned along this axis depending on how their associated ratings relate to age group membership (older or younger adults).

We performed our initial multilevel PLS-DAs through the "mixOmics" R package (Rohart et al., 2017). In each analysis, we inserted observations (i.e., Target Words from older and younger adults) as outcome variables, Dimensions (N = 39) as numerical predictors, Age Group (Older, Younger) as a grouping factor, and the Target Words as multilevel variables. Since older and younger adults provided evaluations on the same wordset, each target word was repeated twice. We ran the multilevel PLS-DAs on centered and standardized variables (i.e., scaled mean scores per word per dimension).

In line with this, 39 Principal Components were extracted. As a further step, for each semantic domain, we estimated the best number of PCs to retain based on different metrics (Maximum Distance, Centroids Distance, and Mahalanobis Distance)-which resulted in one for each of them (PC1 -see section 5.2)-using the perf() function in the "mixOmics" R package, and we ultimately ran the final PLS-DA on such an identified PC.

Since PLS-DA is prone to overfitting (Kjeldahl & Bro, 2010; Westerhuis et al., 2008), we assessed each final model's robustness by performing a cross-validation using the "RVAideMemoire" R package (Hervé, 2022). Specifically, we tested the significance of the model's results by verifying that the observed classification accuracy (Classification Error Rate -CER) was better than expected by chance through 1,000 permutation tests, with comparisons corrected using Bonferroni's method.

In addition, since in each PLS-DA input dataset the mean ratings per word and dimension were derived from a different (though comparable across age groups) number of observations-some of Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts which were relatively low for certain dimensions (i.e., 4-6 per group -see Table S2, SM)-we implemented a (1,000 permutations) proportional bootstrap leave-out approach on each model to ensure that these aspects might not inflate our results, and more broadly to double check models' robustness (for details and results, see Appendix A, SM).

Finally, we explored the amount of variance explained by each PC1, along with the contribution of the distinction between observations in age groups (distributed on opposite sides of PC1) to its organization.

Between-domain semantic similarities within age groups.

We first investigated how similar the semantic domains (i.e., ecological, geo, natural, and technological) were between each other within each age group (older, younger adults), based on participants' ratings. To this end, we compared the structures of the first components (PC1) obtained from each PLS-DA model, with each side of the PC1s predominantly reflecting one of the two age groups (see section 5.2). Pairwise similarities were computed across PC1's loadings using multiple complementary indices: Pearson's Correlation Coefficient, Cosine Similarity, Tucker's Congruence Coefficient, and a Normalized Frobenius Norm.

The Pearson Correlation Coefficient (Pearson) quantifies the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables, ranging from -1 (perfect negative correlation) to 1 (perfect positive correlation) (Pearson, 1909).

The Cosine Similarity (Cosine) measures the similarity between two vectors by computing the cosine of the angle between them. Its value can range between -1 and 1, where values close to 1 indicate that the two vectors point in nearly the same direction-i.e., high similarity-whereas values close to -1 indicate opposite orientations (Han et al., 2012). The Tucker's Congruence Coefficient (Tucker) instead evaluates the similarity between two component loading patterns. Its values can range from 0 (no similarity) to 1 (perfect matching) (Jones et al., 2021; Lorenzo-Seva & ten Berge, 2006).

The Frobenius Norm (Frobenius) quantifies how close two multivariate structures are. We normalized it, and, since larger values represent greater differences, we decided to invert it to express Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts similarity instead, to be consistent with all the other measures. Frobenius values can range from 0 to 1, where values under 0.1 are considered low, suggesting high dissimilarity between matrices; values ranging from 0.1 to 0.5 indicate moderate similarities, while values greater than 0.5 indicate larger correspondence between two matrices (Horn & Johnson, 2012).

In addition, to summarize the overall similarity between each pair of domains based on these metrics, we computed an Averaged Similarity Index (AvgSim) as the arithmetic mean of the four metrics (Pearson, Cosine, Tucker, and Frobenius). The AvgSim ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating stronger overall correspondence across the domains' principal components.

Finally, we applied a Procrustes Test (Protest) to assess whether pairwise semantic configurations shared a statistically reliable geometric structure. Protest is a permutation-based procedure that evaluates how well one configuration can be optimally aligned to another-after rotation, translation, and scaling-and tests whether the observed degree of alignment exceeds what would be expected if the two configurations had no meaningful structural correspondence (Sergeant et al., 2016). We used 1,000 random permutations to derive empirical p-values and a correlation coefficient (for its interpretation, see Tucker's Congruence Coefficient) to assess the significance and strength of the cross-domain structural alignment. Because the four semantic domains yielded six possible pairwise comparisons, p-values from the six Procrustes tests were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Holm procedure (Holm, 1979). The Holm-adjusted p-values were used to determine statistical significance, whereas the AvgSim values were retained as descriptive measures and were not subjected to multiple-comparison correction (see section 5.2).

Within-domain semantic differences across age groups.

Once we assessed the degree of semantic similarity across domains within each age group, we zoomed in on the differences in the conceptualization of each domain by older and younger adults. We did so by exploring, separately for each semantic domain, age group differences in each PC1 composition in terms of complexityi.e., semantic richness and variety-, and concreteness. Specifically, we focused on dimensions with a VIP score higher than 1, and analyzed how they and related components (i.e., "abstractness", Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts "sensorimotor&experiential", "emotional&inner", "social metacognition", "sociopolitical", "impact", "naturalness-artificiality"; see section 3.2.2) contributed, in terms of number and type, to each side of the PC, which predominantly reflected one age group (see section 5.2). In the PLS-DA, the VIP (Variable Importance in Projection) score is a metric used to identify which parameters (in our case, semantic dimensions) contribute most to discriminating between groups (in our case, older and younger adults). The threshold of importance is usually set to > 1: variables with a VIP value greater than 1 are selected, whereas those with a VIP value less than 1 are discarded (Mahieu et al., 2023). In our investigation, we also considered the weight (W, i.e., loadings) of each selected dimension in characterizing each PC1 side, reflecting the domain's representation by one age group (see above). In this context, the weights reflect the contribution and direction of each semantic dimension to PC1, with higher absolute values indicating a stronger role in differentiating between older and younger adults.

To further assess whether the differences observed in the PLS-DA across age groups were reliable, we also fit separate ordinal regression models for each semantic domain. Each model included rating scores as a dependent variable, and the interaction between Age Group (Older, Younger) and Dimensions (N = 39) as a fixed factor. Initially, the models also included Target Words and Participants as random intercepts, but they were discarded due to convergence issues. We estimated the significance of the interactions through Type III ANOVAs. For the sake of conciseness, these models are not reported in the main text but can be found in Appendix B, SM. Appendix C, SM, also reports corresponding mixed-effects models with age entered as a continuous predictor.

Anova and post-hoc comparisons. The ANOVA on the linear model was performed using the "car" R package (Fox & Weisberg, 2019), while ANOVAs on ordinal (mixed) regression models were run using the "RVAideMemoire" R package with p-values calculated using Wald's Chi-squared test. For all statistical models, pairwise post-hoc comparisons to explore main effects and interactions were performed using the "emmeans" R package (Lenth, 2023), with Tukey's adjustments for multiple comparisons.

Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts Plots. All the figures were plotted using "ggplot2" (Wickham, 2016).

5. Results

>Results

5.1. Characteristics of the compared samples of younger and older individuals.

Both statistical models on familiarity and personal experiences yielded a significant interaction between Age Group and Category of Word (Model on Familiarity: X 2 (3) = 234.52, p < .001; Model on Personal Experiences: X 2 (3) = 74.457, p < .001). For familiarity ratings, post-hoc pairwise comparisons revealed that younger adults were more familiar with technological concepts than older adults, SE = 0.599, z = 2.980, p = .035, while no other significant differences emerged, all p s > .367.

For the model on personal experiences, we found that older adults perceived to personally experience ecological concepts significantly more than younger adults, SE = 0.380, z = 2.545, p = .010, and no Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts other differences were found, all p s > .094. Finally, we found no differences between older and younger adults in their level of expertise in green topics, X 2 (1) = 1.1426, p = .285 (see Table S3, SM for descriptive statistics).

Thus, the findings indicate domain-specific age-group differences, with younger adults reporting greater familiarity with technological concepts, while older adults show greater personal experience with ecological concepts.

5.2. PLS-DAs to examine between-and within-domain semantic differences across age groups.

Among the 39 Principal Components extracted from our four initial PLS-DAs, all indexes (i.e., Maximum Distance, Centroids Distance, and Mahalanobis Distance) suggested one as the best number of PCs to retain for all semantic domains. The cross-validation test performed on each final PLS-DA encompassing only the first component (PC1) confirmed each model results' robustness, showing that they significantly differed from chance (Ecological: CER = .044, p < .001; Geo: CER = .095, p < .001; Natural: CER = .061, p < .001; Technological: CER = .018, p < .001, see Appendix A, SM). For both ecological and natural concepts, PC1 explained 41% of the dataset's variance, while for both geo and technological concepts, it accounted for 43% of the variance. In addition, the distinction between older and younger adults completely accounted for explaining all PC1s' organization (100%), with all older and younger adults' ratings lying on opposing sides-arbitrally, older adults on the left, younger adults on the right side of each PC1 (see Figure S1, SM, for a graphic representation of the distribution of target words from older and younger adults in a bidimensional semantic space for each semantic domain).

5.3. Between-domain semantic similarities within age groups.

Pairwise similarity analyses comparing the PC1 structures derived from four domain-specific PLS-DA models, each contrasting older and younger adults, revealed three main patterns (see Figure 2).

The natural and geo domains showed the strongest correspondence (AvgSim = .81), with significant Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts Procrustes alignment (Protest = .32, p < .001). The ecological domain showed intermediate correspondence with both the natural (AvgSim = .59, Protest = .69, p = .001) and geo (AvgSim = .58, Protest = .69, p = .001) domains. In contrast, the technological domain showed substantially lower correspondence with the ecological (AvgSim = .19), geo (AvgSim = .18), and natural (AvgSim = .09) domains, with the lowest similarity observed for the technological-natural comparison; none of these comparisons showed significant Procrustes alignment (all ps > .31). The individual similarity coefficients (i.e., Pearson Correlation, Cosine Similarity, Tucker's Congruence Coefficient, and normalized Frobenius-based similarity) are reported in Table S8, SM. Appendix D, SM, provides an overview of the pairwise domain comparisons plotted in a bidimensional semantic space to visually inspect similarities and differences in the distribution of dimensions associated with the youngerolder adult contrast across domains.

So, to sum up, our findings on between-domain comparisons within age groups reveal a strong correspondence in the semantic structure of natural and geo concepts, with intermediate similarity to ecological concepts, which also refer to the natural environment but mostly in terms of the environmental consequences of human activities. In contrast, the technological domain exhibited substantially lower similarity with all other domains, especially natural, indicating a more distinct semantic structure within age groups.

Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts

5.4. Within-domain semantic differences across age groups.

In the next subsections, we will zoom into each PC1 composition and discuss how ecological (section 5.4.1), geo and natural (section 5.4.2), and technological concepts (section 5.4.3) are characterized as a function of age groups in terms of the complexity and concreteness of semantic representations. We will do so by exploring the number and type of dimensions and components encompassed by each Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts age group PC1 side, along with the weight (W) that each dimension has in characterizing the pole.

Our discussion will focus only on dimensions that statistically distinguish between age groups-i.e., those with a VIP score greater than 1 (see section 4). For an overview of the contribution of all dimensions to each side of the PC1 for each semantic domain, please see Appendix E, SM.

Importantly, we found that older and younger adults differ on these dimensions, as shown in statistical models comparing them on related ratings (see section 4). The full results of these models are available in Appendix B, SM (mixed-effects models with age entered as a continuous predictor, see Appendix C, SM).

5.4.1. Age group differences in the semantic organization of ecological concepts.

For the ecological domain, only 19 of the total 39 dimensions significantly contributed to differentiating the semantic organization of ecological concepts between older and younger adults.

On the resulting PC1 (see Figure 3), we first find that the older adults' side (yellow, left) encompasses more dimensions (n = 14) than the younger adults' side (n = 5, light blue, right). In addition, considering their distribution into components (color-coded in Figure 3), more components appear relevant for older adults to characterize the domain (all except the "social metacognition" component) than for younger adults (all except the "abstractness" and "emotional&inner" components).

Furthermore, each component contains more dimensions for older than younger adults. For instance, in the "sensorimotor" component, 4 dimensions are present for older adults versus only 1 for younger adults. In addition, for both age groups, the "naturalness~artificiality" component did not significantly contribute to the semantic characterization of ecological concepts.

Focusing on the characterization that older adults provided to ecological concepts, we first notice that older adults seem to characterize ecological concepts mainly in a concrete way ("abstractness" component), as referring to something primarily linked to contexts (Context Availability, W = -0.19), evoking bodily interactions (Body-Object Interaction; W = -0.19), easy to define (Easiness of Providing a Definition; W = -0.16), but acquired late in life (Age of Acquisition, W = -0.19). These insights are confirmed by looking at the "sensorimotor&experiential" component, where ecologyrelated entities are perceived by older adults as highly personally experienced (Personal Experience, W = -0.21), and interestingly, experiences happen mainly through bodily parts-particularly through mouth/throat (W = -0.23) feet/legs (W = -0.20), and hands/arms (W = -0.17)-, as opposed to younger adults who seem to mainly experience the domain through taste sensory modality (W = .19).

Older adults also seem to perceive ecological concepts as eliciting a high level of arousal (Arousal, W = -0.21) and as being highly emotionally charged (Emotionality, W = -0.19) ("emotional&inner" component). In addition, older adults appear to conceive them as somewhat negotiable in their meaning (Openness to Negotiation, W = -0.22), and socially relevant (Social Valence, W = -0.17), in contrast with younger adults emphasizing their political relevance (Political Relevance, W = 0.17) ("sociopolitical" component).

Older adults also perceive ecological concepts as highly life-impactful, especially in their present (Perceived Impact in the Present, W = -0.24) and future lives (Perceived Impact in the Future, W = -0.24), as opposed to younger adults considering them as psychologically distant (Perceived Distance, W = 0.23) ("impact" component).

Interestingly, unlike older adults, younger adults seem to rely highly on experts (Expert Social Metacognition, W = 0.22) and generic others (Other Social Metacognition, W = 0.21) to understand the meaning of ecological concepts.

To sum up, age-group differences in the semantic organization of ecological concepts appear more pronounced among older adults, whose representations involve a broader range of semantic dimensions and components. Older adults primarily characterized ecological concepts as concrete, personally experienced, bodily grounded, emotionally and socially relevant, and impactful on their present and future lives. In contrast, younger adults emphasized their political relevance, sensory grounding, psychological distance, and reliance on experts and generic others as sources of knowledge. The geo and natural domains exhibited a highly similar pattern in terms of semantic similarities across the two age groups (see section 5.3), which is why we discuss them together. In their case, only 20 dimensions for geo concepts (see Figure 4) and 18 for natural ones (see Figure 5) significantly contributed to differentiate the semantic organization of the two domains between older and younger adults. Importantly, the characterization of geo and natural concepts was also similar to that of ecological concepts (see section 5.3). Indeed, also in their case, the older adults' PC1 side encompasses more dimensions than that of younger adults (n = 13 vs n = 7 for geo concepts; n = 15 vs n = 3 for natural concepts). In addition, all components (color-coded in Figures 4 and 5) appear relevant to older adults for characterizing both domains, in contrast with the lower component variety shown by younger adults. To illustrate, for younger adults, the "sociopolitical" and "naturalness~artificiality" components are missing to characterize both domains, and, for natural concepts, the "emotional&inner" and "sensorimotor" components as well. Furthermore, each component contains more dimensions for older than younger adults. For instance, the characterization of the "sensorimotor" component by older adults includes 4 dimensions for both geo and natural concepts, whereas for younger adults it encompasses only 2 dimensions for geo concepts and none for natural ones.

Similarly to ecological concepts, older adults seem to stress the concrete peculiarities of geo and natural concepts, representing them as strictly linked to contexts (Context Availability, Geo W = -.23; Natural W = -.24), highly imaginable (Imageability, Geo W = -.22; Natural W = -.23), easy to define (Easiness to Provide a Definition, Geo W = -.21; Natural W = -.21), and natural concepts also frequently encountered (Frequency, Natural W = -.21), as opposed to younger adults who stress more their mostly linguistic modality of acquisition (Modality of Acquisition, Geo W = .17; Natural W = .20) ("abstractness" component).

Related to this, ratings of older adults reveal that they personally experience both domains (Personal Experience, Geo W = -.17; Natural W = -.18), with experiences that happen mainly through bodily Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts parts-mainly via mouth/throat (Geo W = -.22; Natural W = -.23), but also feet/legs (Geo W = -.17; Natural W = -.20) and hands/arms (Geo W = -.18; Natural W = -.17). On the other hand, younger adults consider more important sensory modalities, but only for geo concepts-specifically touch (W = .20) and taste (W = .18) ("sensorimotor" component).

Older adults also empathize the high emotional load of both domains (Emotionality, Geo W = -.24; Natural W = -.23), while younger adults perceive geo concepts as eliciting arousal (W = .21) ("emotional&inner" component).

For both domains, ratings of younger adults highlight the importance of relying on field experts (Expert Social Metacognition, Geo W = .24; Natural W = .24) and also generic others just for geo concepts (Other Social Metacognition, W = .17) to understand geo and natural concepts' meaning ("social metacognition" component).

In addition, older adults rated geo and natural concepts as highly politically relevant (Political Relevance, Geo W = -.19; Natural W = -.20) and socially salient (Social Valence, Geo W = -.20; Natural W = -.23) ("sociopolitical" component). Linked to this, older adults consider geo and natural concepts as highly impactful in their present (Perceived Impact in the Present, Geo W = -.17; Natural W = -.21) and future life (Perceived Impact in the Future, Geo W = -.17; Natural W = -.21) and natural concepts also in their past life (Perceived Impact in the Past, W = -.19), while younger adults stress more the psychological distance felt from them (Geo W = .23; Natural W = .25) ("impact" component).

Finally, older adults also emphasize the scientific character of both geo and natural concepts (Scientificity, Geo W = -.19; Natural W = -.25) ("naturalness~artificiality" component).

To summarize, the geo and natural domains show highly similar age group patterns, characterized by a broader, more concrete, and multidimensional semantic representation among older adults. Older adults emphasized the concrete, personally experienced and bodily grounded, emotionally, politically and socially salient, life-impactful, and scientific aspects of these concepts. In contrast, younger adults placed greater emphasis on the linguistic modality of concept acquisition, sensory grounding, reliance on social sources of knowledge (both experts and others), and the psychological distance they felt from these concepts.
