5.4.3. Age group differences in the semantic organization of technological concepts.

Similarly to ecological concepts, only 19 of the total 39 dimensions significantly contributed to differentiate the semantic characterization of technological concepts between older and younger adults. The resulting PC1 (see Figure 6) shows that technological concepts exhibit, overall, a more diverse age group pattern than green concepts (see also section 5.3). Indeed, in their case, the number of components that significantly distinguish between the two age groups does not differ substantially between older and younger adults (n = 11 vs n = 8), nor does the number of dimensions contributing to each component.

Zooming into their semantic characterization across age groups, we first notice that older adults rate technological concepts as acquired late (Age of Acquisition, W = -.23) and frequently encountered in daily life (Frequency, W = -.22), and, interestingly, although they rated technological concepts as mostly abstract (Concreteness~Abstractness, W = -.19), they also stress the possibility to physically interact with their referent (Body-Object Interaction, W = -.17). In opposition, younger adults conceive technological concepts with more marked concrete peculiarities related to word mastering, describing them as familiar (Familiarity, W = 0.21) and easy to define (Easiness of Providing a Definition, W = .21) ("abstractness" component). In the same vein, younger adults conceive technological concepts as being well-mastered by both themselves (Word Confidence, W = .23) and field experts (Confidence in Experts, W = .17), as opposed to older adults who instead feel they need the help of others to understand tech-meaning (Other Social Metacognition, W = -.20) ("social metacognition" component).

These differences seem to be well-expressed in the main sensorimotor aspects elicited by technological concepts in the distinct age groups: while older adults give more importance to the mouth/throat activation (W = -.21), younger adults consider the hands/arms involvement (W = .20) more salient ("sensorimotor" component).

In addition, older adults also stress the high emotional charge of technological concepts (Emotionality, W = -.23); in contrast, younger adults conceive technological concepts as activating interoceptive aspects (Interoception, W = .24) ("emotional&inner" component).

Social linguistic exchanges appear important for both age groups, but while older adults mainly emphasize the possibility of negotiating technological concepts' meaning with others (Openness to Negotiation, W = -.18), younger adults conceive technological concepts as a good starting point for a conversation (Easiness to Start a Conversation, W = .22) ("sociopolitical" component).

Additionally, older adults focus more on the relevance of technologies in their present (Perceived Impact in the Present, W = -.16) and future lives (Perceived Impact in the Future, W = -.19), while younger adults consider them more impactful in their past (Perceived Impact in the Past, W = .16) ("impact" component). Finally, older adults also emphasize the scientific nature of technological concepts (Scientificity, W = -.19) ("naturalness~artificiality" component).

To sum up, technological concepts show a more balanced pattern of age group differentiation than green concepts, with older and younger adults contributing a relatively similar number of components and semantic dimensions. Older adults characterized technological concepts as acquired relatively late in life and frequently encountered in everyday contexts, while simultaneously perceiving them as relatively abstract yet physically interactable. They also emphasized their emotional and scientific character, as well as their relevance to present and future life, and showed greater activation of the mouth/throat bodily region, potentially linked to their greater reliance on others, through speech, to understand and negotiate the meaning of technological concepts. In contrast, younger adults emphasized technological concepts as familiar, easy to define, and well mastered by both themselves and field experts, with greater reliance on sensory grounding through the hands and arms and on interoceptive experiences. They also viewed technological concepts as more readily conducive to conversation and as more impactful in their past lives.

6. Discussion

Overall, our results suggest that age group differences play a key role in explaining variations in the semantic representation across conceptual domains. Consistent with this, separating participants into younger and older adults accounted for a substantial proportion of the variance in the PLS-DA analyses of our rating data (PC1: 41% for ecological and natural concepts; 43% for geo and technological concepts).

In line with our experimental hypotheses (see section 1.2), we first found that, within each age group, semantic representations were more similar across green domains and more differentiated when compared with the technological domain. Specifically, between-domain pairwise similarity comparisons (see section 5.3) showed that green concepts cluster together semantically, especially geo and natural, with ecological concepts slightly more distinct but still aligned. The technological domain, by contrast, showed minimal similarity with any green domain for either age group, and displays no significant structural alignment, especially in its comparison with natural concepts-a finding supporting the usually investigated distinction between artifacts and natural kinds (Chen et al., 2016; Forde & Humphreys, 2005; Warrington & Shallice, 1984).

When zooming in on the semantic characterization of each domain (see section 5.4), interesting age group differences emerged. First, in line with our hypotheses (see section 1.2), across the green domains, older adults consistently showed a richer and more variegated semantic organization than younger adults, drawing on a larger number of dimensions overall and within each component, and on a greater number of contributing components. In addition, although both older and younger adults seem to characterize green concepts as hybrid in terms of abstractness-i.e., including both abstract and concrete features (Falcinelli et al., 2024a)-older adults' conceptualization appears more concrete and experientially grounded. For instance, older adults rated all green concepts as more contextually linked, easier to define, and more evocative of personal experiences than younger adults (Falcinelli et al., 2024a; Paivio, 1990; Schwanenflugel et al., 1992; see also Appendix B, SM).

Importantly, older adults' experiences with green referents mainly involve bodily effectors-i.e., Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts mouth/throat, hands/arms, and feet/legs-across all domains (Lynott et al., 2020). Alongside these concrete features, older adults also attribute high emotional charge and social relevance to green concepts, aspects usually associated with abstract concepts (Diveica et al., 2023 (Diveica et al., , 2025;; Ponari et al., 2018). Finally, older adults consider green concepts highly impactful in their lives, particularly in the present and future. Altogether, these characteristics point to a hybrid but mostly concrete, variegated, experience-rich, and personally meaningful representation of green concepts in older adults.

In contrast, younger adults appear to conceptualize ecological, geo, and natural concepts in a hybrid manner, but one that is slightly more abstract and more cognitively mediated and distant. To illustrate, like typical abstract concepts, the representations of green concepts by younger adults highly rely on socio-metacognitive aspects, such as the need to consult experts and generic others (just for ecological and geo concepts) to understand conceptual meaning; in addition, younger adults also conceive green concepts as psychological distant (Borghi, 2022; Falcinelli et al., 2024a; Mazzuca et al., 2022). At the same time, similarly to more concrete concepts, sensorimotor aspects also count for younger adults, but their importance is limited to a few sensory modalities and not for all green domains (Lynott & Connell, 2013)-i.e., taste for ecological and geo concepts, and additionally touch only for geo concepts. These findings might suggest a more passive way of experiencing green referents in younger adults compared to the more active, bodily, and motor-based activation of older adults.

Overall, these findings may reflect qualitative differences in the kinds of real-world experiences each age group has with green domains: older adults' richer, more variegated, and concrete representations align with greater experiential involvement with the natural environment, whereas younger adults' more informationally mediated representations reflect their more limited direct engagement (Ágoston et al., 2024). This is in line with previous findings showing more involvement in green activities and greater pro-environmental behavioral tendencies in older compared to younger adults (López-Mosquera et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021), which potentially lead to more concrete conceptualizations (Falcinelli et al., 2025a).

Importantly, although all concepts within the green domain are highly semantically aligned, finegrained differences emerge in how older and younger adults conceptualize ecological concepts compared to geographical and natural ones (see also section 5.3). For instance, older adults place greater emphasis on the later age of acquisition of ecological concepts and on the possibility of interacting with their referents, while highlighting the greater imaginability of geo-and naturalconceptual domains. Older adults also emphasize the political relevance of geo and natural concepts, whereas this aspect appears more salient for ecological concepts among younger adults. In addition, older adults report higher levels of arousal for ecological concepts, as they seem more open to negotiating their meanings with others; instead, they place greater emphasis on the scientific nature of geo and natural concepts. Similarly, younger adults stress the predominantly linguistic acquisition of geo and natural concepts, and report higher arousal for geo concepts compared to ecological ones.

In contrast, the technological domain showed a more diverse age group pattern than the green domains, partially confirming our hypotheses (see section 1.2). First, contrary to our expectations, we found that older and younger adults did not consistently differ in the richness and variety of semantic representations of technological concepts-indeed, the number of dimensions and components contributing to their characterization did not differ significantly across age groups. In addition, the representation of technological concepts appeared hybrid for both age groups, but slightly more concrete in younger adults, in line with our hypotheses and with previous research (Falcinelli et al., 2024b). To illustrate, younger adults' representation of technological concepts appears concrete in relation to aspects linked to word meaning mastering: for younger adults, technological concepts are perceived as familiar (Barca et al., 2002) and easy to define (Falcinelli et al., 2024a), a data consistent with the high degree of confidence younger adults perceive in themselves and in field experts when it comes to mastering technology (Mazzuca et al., 2022).

In addition, as for typical concrete concepts, technological concepts evoke sensorimotor aspects, particularly hands/arms bodily parts (Lynott et al., 2020), likely reflecting habitual interactions of younger adults with digital devices (e.g., typing, touching screens, swiping, gaming). At the same time, as is the case with more typical abstract concepts, technological concepts activate interoceptive processes in younger adults (Connell et al., 2018; Villani et al., 2019 Villani et al., , 2021) ) and are considered good starting points for conversations (Fini et al., 2023).

Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts Conversely, older adults provide a hybrid but mainly more abstract characterization of technological concepts. For instance, they explicitly rate them as abstract (Paivio, 1990) and perceive technological concepts as highly emotionally charged (Ponari et al., 2018; Vigliocco et al., 2014; Villani et al., 2019). At the same time, more concrete aspects also emerge: older adults emphasize the possibility of physically interacting with technological tools (Bennett et al., 2011) and report greater involvement of the mouth/throat (Lynott et al., 2020). The reliance on such sensorimotor bodily parts, as opposed to the hands' grounding in younger adults, suggests that older adults might understand technology primarily through social-linguistic scaffolding rather than direct manipulation. We can speculate that this pattern might point to a form of social metacognition in older adults regarding technology: a tendency to engage others in conversation about technological tools, to seek explanations or assistance, and to learn through verbal interaction-by naming, describing, and discussing functions and features. Supporting this idea, our data reveals that older adults show a high openness to negotiating technological concepts' meaning and express a strong need to rely on others to understand them, as it is typical of more abstract concepts (Borghi, 2022; Fini et al., 2023)-perhaps also because they conceive technological concepts as highly scientific. In addition, older adults emphasize the late acquisition of technological concepts and the frequency and relevance of technology for their present and future lives. Altogether, this data suggests that while older adults could still be in the process of learning how to use technological devices-also thanks to the help of others through linguistic exchanges-younger adults, who have grown up with them, might already be skilled users (indeed, they report a high level of confidence with the domain), and thus take their presence more for granted.

In support of this, the younger sample emphasizes the role that technological devices played in their past.

Notably, in our study, we also separately examined differences between older and younger adults in their levels of familiarity and personal experience with all targeted domains, as reflected in their ratings (see section 5.1). Results showed that older adults reported greater personal experience with the ecological domain, whereas younger adults reported greater familiarity with the technological domain. This pattern is consistent with the relevance of these dimensions in characterizing our PLS-Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts DAs: there, we found that personal experience accounted highly (W = -.21) in shaping the semantic organization of the ecological domain by older adults, while familiarity (W = -.21) greatly accounted for characterizing the technological domain for younger adults (see Figures 3 and 6).

These findings lead to speculation on the distinct role of these factors in shaping the age-dependent semantic characterization of the two domains. Age group differences in the representation of ecological concepts may reflect more qualitative variations driven by the presence of direct personal experiences with the domain (see above), whereas differences in the representation of technological concepts may perhaps reflect more quantitative variations in the frequency, continuity, and diversity of exposure-that is, familiarity-with the domain. For example, both younger and older adults likely use digital devices in their everyday lives (Olson et al., 2011). However, younger adults, having grown up in increasingly digital environments, may have been exposed to a wider range of technological devices over a longer period, leading to greater familiarity and confidence. This sustained engagement may, in turn, have fostered a more concrete and usage-based representation in this group, in contrast to the more abstract, socially scaffolded, and affectively marked representations observed in older adults.

Hence, although we did not directly test the influence of these aspects on semantic representations, we may hypothesize that the semantic complexity and concreteness of conceptual domains may not be shaped solely by age per se, but rather by factors associated with age group membership, such as differences in the amount and type of exposure to specific domains.

To conclude, our results suggest that the complexity and concreteness of conceptual representations are domain-dependent. In the case of our targeted domains, these aspects appear to interact with age.

In particular, the experiential richness, variability, and concreteness characterizing older adults' representations of green concepts mirror the similarly rich and multifaceted, yet more concrete representations that younger adults display for technological concepts. Older adults' greater lifelong engagement with ecological, geo, and natural contexts-as widely documented in the literature (Ágoston et al., 2024; Falcinelli et al., 2025a; López-Mosquera et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021)-may result in richer, more complex, and more concrete domain representations.

Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts Conversely, younger adults may have developed more concrete representations of technological concepts through their continuous and frequent immersion, since they were born in digital environments (e.g., Falcinelli et al., 2024b; Hunsaker & Hargittai, 2018).

Taken together, our findings highlight the flexibility of the human conceptual system, showing that separate domains exhibit distinct semantic organizations and that individuals across different age groups represent them differently in terms of complexity and concreteness. These differences may also reflect peculiar age group patterns of life experience and domain familiarity, embedded within a specific socio-cultural and historical context.

7. Conclusion and Study Implications and Limits

With this study, we investigated differences between older and younger individuals in their semantic organization of green (ecological, geo, natural) and technological concepts, which belong to domains highly relevant in contemporary society but not yet extensively investigated.

First, our results revealed that within each age group, semantic representations were almost similar among the green domains-particularly between geo and natural concepts-and markedly different between them and the technological domain. This was especially evident when comparing technological concepts with natural ones, closely following the classical distinction between artifacts and natural kinds (Chen et al., 2016; Forde & Humphreys, 2005; Warrington & Shallice, 1984).

By zooming into the semantic composition of each conceptual domain, our results revealed systematic differences in how green and technological concepts were conceptualized by older and younger adults. In the green domains, older adults consistently showed a richer and more multifaceted characterization than younger adults. At the same time, ecological concepts displayed domainspecific nuances that further distinguished them from concepts strictly referring to the natural environment (geo, natural). In contrast, older and younger adults did not differ markedly in the complexity of the characterization of technological concepts. Integrating these findings, although Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts both age groups depicted all domains as hybrid in terms of abstractness-combining both concrete and abstract features (Falcinelli et al., 2024a)-older adults tended to represent green concepts more concretely, whereas younger adults provided a more concrete characterization to technological concepts (Falcinelli et al., 2024b; Falcinelli et al., 2025a). To explain this data, we also found that older adults reported personally experiencing more ecological topics, while younger adults perceived greater familiarity with technological ones. This supports the hypothesis that whereas age group differences in green concepts' semantic organization might reflect more qualitative divergences related to the presence of personal experiences with the domain, differences in technological concepts' characterization might instead reflect more quantitative differences in the frequency, continuity and variety of exposure-that is, familiarity-with the domain, net of a similar presence of personal experiences with technological tools by both age groups.

Hence, as a whole, our findings document that the semantic complexity and concreteness of conceptual representations vary across domains and that these variations depend on the interaction of many factors, such as the age group membership and all that it entails, like different levels of life experience and familiarity with a domain.

Despite the interesting insights, our study presents some limitations that should be acknowledged for future research on the topic. Some of them concern the word pool and the task. Firstly, the word size for each kind of concept is lower compared to similar studies on semantic norms (e.g., Bennett et al., 2011; Brysbaert et al., 2014; Diveica et al., 2023; Lynott & Connell, 2013; Lynott et al., 2020; Tillotson et al., 2008; for Italian examples, see Della Rosa et al., 2010; De Varda et al., 2025; Montefinese et al., 2014; Repetto et al., 2023; Villani et al., 2019), but we targeted several semantic dimensions. In addition, while being highly representative examples for each semantic domain (see Falcinelli et al., 2024a), the words selected for each class represent only one of the possible infinite sub-samples. Third, although we checked the robustness and stability of our results (see Appendix A, SM), they were based on different numbers of ratings per dimension and age group. Altogether, these aspects might affect the generalizability of our findings to the whole semantic domain.

Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts

In addition, although rating tasks are widely used to investigate semantic representations (e.g., Barca et al., 2002; Bennett et al., 2011; Brysbaert et al., 2014; Della Rosa et al., 2010; Diveica et al., 2023; Lynott et al., 2020; Lynott & Connell, 2013; Montefinese et al., 2014; Repetto et al., 2023; Tillotson et al., 2008), relying exclusively on explicit judgments may overlook further interesting aspects concerning conceptualization. In this regard, future studies may integrate implicit behavioral measures (e.g., reaction times, kinematic indexes, and semantic fluency), neurophysiological techniques (e.g., EEG, fNIRS, and physiological devices), or multimethod and more sophisticated approaches to gain a more comprehensive understanding of differences in domains' semantic representations across age groups (for some insights, see Falcinelli et al., 2025b). In this respect, the O-TECo database might offer valuable linguistic material for designing such investigations.

However, semantic norms we collected are likely to be intrinsically sensitive to contextual fluctuations, making them prone to instability and requiring periodic updates to maintain reliability and validity.

Other criticalities concern the sample. First, we targeted only two broad age groups-older and younger adults-whereas more fine-grained evidence could be obtained by including additional subgroups spanning the entire lifespan, from children to centenarians. In addition, our study is crosssectional, an aspect that prevents us from directly addressing developmental trajectories in conceptual representations.

Second, data were collected from Italian participants. Given that the domains we examinedparticularly ecological and technological ones-are highly sensitive to sociocultural and sociopolitical contexts, and that conceptualizations may vary across languages and cultures (e.g., Borghi & Mazzuca, 2023; Lewis et al., 2023; Mazzuca et al., 2024), our findings may not generalize beyond the specific temporal and contextual setting in which they were obtained. In this sense, the observed age group differences should be interpreted as a snapshot of a particular time and context and may vary across cultures and historical periods. Consequently, they may not extend to the broader Western world, nor to populations beyond WEIRD samples (Henrich & Norenzayan, 2010), or to individuals of similar age profiles embedded in different historical periods. In addition, the sample Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts has not been balanced with respect to educational level, geographic region within Italy (see Table S3, SM), and digital literacy. These characteristics may be relevant to the semantic dimensions investigated here, and need to be addressed in future studies: educational background and digital literacy may shape familiarity with and ways of conceptualizing technological concepts, whereas geographic and sociocultural differences within Italy may contribute to variability in experiences with and representations of green concepts, particularly ecological ones.

Moreover, individual differences in attitudes, beliefs, expertise, and experience may shape the representation of the targeted concepts. Previous work has shown that conceptual representations can vary as a function of expertise, experience, and attitudes toward the relevant domains (e.g., Blasi et al., 2022; Buchanan et al., 2021; Croijmans et al., 2020; Falcinelli et al., 2024b; Falcinelli et al., 2025a; Mazzuca et al., 2024; Purves et al., 2023; Villani et al., 2021 Villani et al., , 2022)). For instance, climatechange attitudes vary by age, education, socioeconomic characteristics, political orientation, and broader sociocultural factors (Czarnek et al., 2021; Pinna et al., 2024; Di Gessa & Zaninotto, 2026), potentially contributing to cohort-related differences in how ecological concepts are experienced and represented. Religious affiliation, also, may also contribute to shaping ecological representations. For instance, Ecker et al. (2024) found that Roman Catholics in Latin America were less likely to acknowledge the anthropogenic origins of climate change than individuals belonging to other religious denominations or reporting no religious affiliation. Such factors may therefore contribute to differences in the complexity and concreteness of semantic representations across age groups.

However, we did not systematically assess these variables-aside from a limited set of demographic characteristics (see sections 3.3, 4, and 5.1)-and therefore cannot determine their contribution to the observed age-group differences. This limitation is particularly relevant given evidence that conceptual representations are partly individual-specific (Botch & Finn, 2024), suggesting that personal experience and other individual-level characteristics such as beliefs may modulate the relationship between age and semantic representation.

Despite the limitations, our study entails several important implications. From a theoretical side, our results are relevant for research on categorization and conceptual abstractness, highlighting the flexibility of the human conceptual system (e.g., Barsalou, 1993; Connell & Lynott, 2014; Mazzuca et al., 2021 Mazzuca et al., , 2022)), and showing that concepts, even if of recent appearance like ecological and technological ones, can be characterized differently as a function of different age groups.

In addition, our findings contribute to jeopardizing classic theories on concepts that rely on a strict opposition between abstract and concrete concepts (e.g., Barsalou & Wiemer-Hastings, 2005) by integrating more recent evidence attesting a mixed characterization between abstract and concrete concepts for some conceptual kinds (e.g., gender : Mazzuca et al., 2020 : Mazzuca et al., , 2024;; odor: Majid et al., 2018). Overall, these and our findings contribute to substantiate more recent theories on concepts (e.g., Barsalou et al., 2018; Borghi, 2022 Borghi, , 2023;; Crutch et al., 2013; Dove, 2022; Reilly et al., 2025) which propose to study conceptual kinds beyond abstractness, conceiving conceptual representations as multidimensional structures constituted by different components (e.g., sensorimotor, emotional, inner, sociopolitical) and investigating how specific conceptual domains locate in their space-as we did in our work.

Finally, our results also have implications for the lifespan and aging literature, providing a first systematic and analytical assessment of how older adults represent specific conceptual domains compared to younger adults (Borghi & Setti, 2017; Costello et al., 2017; Costello et al., 2025).

On a societal side, being aware of the differences between older and younger adults in representing green and technological concepts might be useful to implement more age-idiosyncratic interventions aimed at allowing a better population adherence to political advice on environmental protection or technology use, and addressing each age group's specific difficulties and needs, thus enhancing human and environmental wellness.

Finally, on the scientific side, the O-TECo database resulting from our study, freely available to the scientific community (see section 2), can be used by researchers to select linguistic stimuli for further studies on these topics. Indeed, we believe our work can serve as a good starting point for future research aimed at deepening understanding of how different age groups conceptualize and relate to these timely domains, giving voice to their singular perspectives and experiences embedded in specific socio-cultural and historical contexts.

was removed from the high-N dimensions (up to 16 ratings per dimension-because the minimum number of ratings in the low-N dimensions was 4), while the low-N dimensions were kept intact.

This approach was chosen to ensure that the more sparsely rated dimensions would not, again, drive the resampling-induced variability. In addition, because the two groups contributed the same number of ratings to every dimension in the original dataset, we removed an equal number of observations from younger and older participants in each bootstrap iteration. This prevented the procedure from altering the original symmetry between groups and ensured that the variability introduced through subsampling reflected only withindimension variation rather than artificial changes in group composition. After each subsampling step, we recomputed the dimension means, reconstructed the data matrices, and refit the PLS-DA model under identical settings.

For every iteraction, we extracted the loading vector and VIP scores and compared them with the loadings from the corresponding full model. Procrustes Test, quantifying geometric similarity after optimal rotation, translation, and scaling (for details on these metrics, see section 4). We repeated this procedure 1,000 times to ensure robust, reliable estimates of model stability.

Finally, we descriptively compared the five metrics obtained from the model, including all dimensions and the model with only high-N dimensions. This comparison served as an indirect indicator: if the stability metrics were very similar between these two models, it suggested that the low-N dimensions did not significantly influence the PLS-DA results, confirming that our full model with all dimensions could be reliably used.

Across the ecological, technological, and geo domains, the bootstrap analyses provided strong evidence of robustness and structural stability of the PLS-DAs, revealing a high correspondence between the full models and the bootstrap iterations. For the ecological domain,

Pearson Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts Correlations between the bootstrap and full-model loadings reached 0.84 (all dimensions) and 0.84 (high-N only). Cosine Similarities were 0.87 in both cases, Tucker's Congruence Coefficients 0.87, Frobenius Norm 0.51, and Procrustes Tests 0.30-values nearly identical across models. The technological domain showed a similarly robust profile (Pearson: 0.85; Cosine: 0.85; Tucker: 0.85; Frobenius: 0.54; Procrustes: 0.27, for both all dimensions and high-N models). The geo domain also displayed matched metrics (Pearson: 0.82; Cosine: 0.84; Tucker: 0.84; Frobenius: 0.57; Procrustes: 0.32, for both all dimensions and high-N models).

The high value of these metrics and the similarity in results of "all dimensions" and "high-N" models confirmed the stability and robustness of the full models and indicated that the inclusion of low-N dimensions did not materially affect the PLS-DA outcomes for any semantic domain, supporting the use of the complete model for our data explorations.

In contrast, the natural domain exhibited a somewhat divergent pattern. While still stable, the similarity metrics indicated slightly greater variability in loading structure relative to the other domains. Pearson Correlations were 0.73 (all dimensions) and 0.70 (high-N only), and Cosine Similarity values mirrored this pattern (all dimensions: 0.76; high-N only: 0.72); Tucker's Congruence Coefficients showed the same trend (all dimensions: 0.76; high-N only: 0.72), suggesting moderate-but still acceptable-structural similarity. In contrast, Frobenius Norms (all dimensions: 0.64; high-N only: 0.67) and Procrustes Tests (all dimensions and high-N only: 0.35) remained low and nearly identical, indicating that the global geometry of the latent space was preserved even when directional agreement declined. This data suggests that the natural domain appears somewhat more sensitive to sampling perturbation, but still displays a stable and interpretable latent pattern. In addition, in this case too, minimal differences in metrics' values between the "all dimensions" and "high-N only" models were found, suggesting that maintaining low-N dimensions in the statistical model does not compromise stability.

Taken as a whole, the bootstrap results confirm that the PLS-DA models we carried out are robust across all domains. The minimal differences found between the full ("all dimensions") and high-N models indicate that including low-N dimensions does not affect stability, supporting the use Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts of the complete models for all domains for a comprehensive representation of the semantic space without compromising methodological soundness.

Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts ecological concepts as more scientific (Scientificity, z = 2.556, SE = .156, p < .0001) and as referring more to artificial entities (Naturalness~Artificiality, z = 5.729, SE = .086, p < .0001) than younger adults.

On the other hand, younger adults perceive ecological concepts as psychologically farther (Perceived Distance, z = 13.842, SE = .099, p < .0001), more politically relevant (Political Relevance, z = 7.620, SE = .078, p < .0001), and they report a higher need to rely on experts (Expert Social Metacognition, z = 7.358, SE = .132, p < .0001)-that they trust more (Confidence in Experts, z = 2.626, SE = .078, p = .008)-, and generic others (Other Social Metacognition, z = 7.627, SE = .080, p < .0001) to understand their meaning.

Finally, compared to younger adults, older adults perceive ecological concepts as more familiar (Familiarity, z = 2.997, SE = .805, p = .002), acquired mainly through linguistic than sensorimotor experiences (Modality of Acquisition, z = 2.516, SE = .094, p = .011), less experienced through the Hearing sensory modality (z = -2.030, SE = -.207, p = .042), and more positively valenced (Valence, z = 2.061, SE = .085, p = .039).

Instead, no differences emerged between older and younger adults in the level of abstractness attributed to ecological concepts (Concreteness~Abstractness), in how confidently they think that they master ecological referents' meaning (Word Confidence), in how much they perceive control on them (Dominance), in the frequency of use of these words (Frequency), and in their activation of interoceptive processes (Interoception) and of the Smell sensory modality, all ps > .231.

Geo and Natural concepts. Both statistical models yielded a significant interaction between Age Group and Dimensions, Geo: X 2 (38) = 2150.4, p < .0001; Natural: X 2 (38) = 1957.1, p < .0001. Pairwise posthoc comparisons showed that compared to younger adults, older adults consider both natural and geo concepts as more linked to contexts (Context Availability, Geo: z = 14.566, SE = .111, p < .0001; Natural: z = 15.815, SE = .113, p < .0001), more imaginable (Imageability, Geo: z = 14.769, SE = .113, p < .0001; Natural: z = 17.099, SE = .121, p < .0001), more frequently encountered (Frequency, Geo: z = 2.766, SE = .130, p = .005; Natural: z = 5.161, SE = .129, p < .0001), and easier to define (Easiness to Provide a Definition, Geo: z = 8.204, SE = .080, p < .0001: Natural: z = 7.044, SE = .086, p < .0001), as opposed to younger adults who perceive them as more linguistically acquired (Modality of Acquisition, Geo: z = 6.191, SE = .092, p < .0001; Natural: z = 10.545, SE = .094, p < .0001), and only geo concepts with a later age of acquisition (Age of Acquisition, z = 3.376, SE = .086, p < .001). Related to this, older adults perceive more the possibility to experience both the domains (Personal Experience, Geo: z = 4.820, SE = .082, p < .0001;

Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts SE = .079, p < .0001; Natural: z = 12.361, SE = .081, p < .0001), and they also rate to be more open to negotiate with others geo concepts' meaning (z = 3.730, SE = .173, p < .001). In addition, compared to younger adults, older adults rated both conceptual domains as more scientific (Scientificity, Geo: z = 4.609, SE = .168, p < .0001; Natural: z = 7.948, SE = .165, p < .0001) and natural concepts as more artificial (Naturalness~Artificiality, z = 4.236, SE = .113, p < .0001).

Finally, compared to younger adults, older adults perceive both natural and geo as a better starting point for a conversation (Easiness to Start a Conversation, Geo: z = 3.134, SE = .138, p = .001; Natural: z = 2.975, SE = .138, p = .002) and while they conceive natural concepts as eliciting the Hearing sensory modality to a greater extent than younger adults (z = 2.047, SE = 1.000, p = .040), they perceive geo concepts as more natural (Naturalness~Artificiality, z = -2.990, SE = .976, p = .002), and they feel more open to negotiate their meaning with others (Openness to Negotiation, z = 3.730, SE = .173, p = .002).

Instead, for both natural and geo concepts, no differences emerged between older and younger adults in their level of abstractness (Concreteness~Abstractness), in the possibility to interact with their referents (Body-Object Interaction), in their Familiarity, in their activation of mental processes (Metacognition), and in their activation of the Smell sensory modality. Exclusively for natural concepts, no differences across age groups were also found in their Age of Acquisition, in the extent to which they are perceived under control (Dominance), in their activation of interoceptive processes (Interoception), in the openness both age groups feel to negotiate their meaning (Openness to Negotiation), in their activation of Taste and Vision sensory modalities, and in their Valence. Exclusively for geo concepts, no differences across age groups also emerged in how confidently older and younger adults think themselves (Word Confidence) and field experts (Confidence in Experts) master their meaning, and in their activation of Hearing sensory modality (Geo: ps > .060; Natural: all ps > .052).

Technological concepts.

The statistical model yielded a significant interaction between Age Group and Dimensions, X 2 (38) = 2744.8, p < .0001. Pairwise post-hoc comparisons showed that compared to older adults, younger adults perceive technological concepts as more familiar (Familiarity, z = 9.265, SE = .082, p < .0001), easier to define (Easiness of Providing a Definition, z = 16.925, SE = .080, p < .0001), and better mastered in their meaning by both themselves (Word Confidence, z = 19.182, SE = .081, p < .0001) and field experts (Confidence in Experts, z = 3.913, SE = .082, p < .001), as opposed to older adults who refer a

Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts higher need to rely on others to understand their meaning (Other Social Metacognition, z = 8.888, SE = .081, p < .0001). In addition, older adults conceive technological concepts as later acquired (Age of Acquisition, z = 22.644, SE = .127, p < .0001) and more through language (Modality of Acquisition, z = 6.568, SE = .095, p < .0001) than younger adults, more frequently encountered (Frequency, z = 8.104, SE = .132, p < .0001), and more abstract (Concreteness~Abstractness, z = 9.110, SE = .082, p < .0001), although they perceive more than the younger sample the possibility to interact with their referents (Body-Object Interaction, z = 4.486, SE = .107, p < .0001).

By contrast, younger adults conceive technological concepts as more positively valenced (Valence, z = 2.844, SE = .070, p = .004), and activating more mental processes (Metacognition, z = 4.173, SE = .084, p < .0001) and inner aspects (Interoception, z = 14.036, SE = .089, p < .0001; Arousal, z = 2.988, SE = .132, p = .002), in opposition with older adults who consider technological concepts as more emotionally charged (Emotionality, z = 13.270, SE = .088, p < .0001).

In addition, while younger adults rated technological concepts as more relevant in their past life (Perceived Impact in the Past, z = 9.390, SE = .082, p < .0001), older adults consider them more impactful in their present (Perceived Impact in the Present, z = 6.900, SE = .080, p < .0001) and future lives (Perceived Impact in the Future, z = 9.343, SE = .083, p < .0001).

As for the sensorimotor aspects, technological concepts activate more the hands/harms (z = 9.428, SE = .086, p < .0001), the torso bodily part (z = 3.130, SE = .090, p = .001) and the touch sensory modality (z = 6.979, SE = .105, p < .0001) in younger adults, while primarily the mouth/throat (z = 7.377, SE = .089, p < .0001) and the hearing sensory modality (z = 4.235, SE = .101, < = .0001) in older adults.

As for sociopolitical aspects, older adults consider technological concepts as more negotiable in their meaning (Openness to Negotiation, z = 2.672, SE = .167, p = .007), while younger adults conceive them more relevant in society (Social Valence, z = 5.222, SE = .081, p < .0001), and a better starting point for a conversation (Easiness to Start a Conversation, z = 8.955, SE = .133, p < .0001).

In addition, older adults perceive technological concepts as more scientific (Scientificity, z = 2.136, SE = .168, p = .032), and younger adults as more artificial (Naturalness~Artificiality, z = 4.289, SE = .147, p < .0001).

Finally, compared to younger adults, older adults perceive technological tools as more linked to contexts (Context Availability, z = 4.694, SE = .108, p < .0001), more under control (Dominance, z = 3.049, SE = Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts

Assessing the robustness and stability of our PLS-DA models using a proportional leave-out bootstrap approach across ecological, geo, natural, and technological concepts.

To evaluate the robustness of the PLS-DA models across the four semantic domains (ecological, geo, natural, and technological), we implemented a proportional leave-one-out bootstrap procedure (e.g., Royston & Sauerbrei, 2009 3 ) using a customized R script. We decided to perform this additional analysis primarily because some dimensions in our dataset (n = 7) had very few ratings (i.e., 4 ratings per group for 2 dimensions; 6 ratings per group for 5 dimensions). We reasoned that these sparse dimensions could inflate or destabilize our multivariate solutions, affecting both the estimated principal component and the interpretation of dimension loadings.

Thus, the goal of the bootstrap procedure was twofold: I) to assess how stable and robust the PLS-DA model remained when the data were perturbed through systematic subsampling, and II) to determine whether it might be appropriate to retain dimensions with a low number of ratings (from now on, "low-N" dimensions) in the final analyses.

We started the procedure by fitting a full PLS-DA model (only on the first PC) for each domain, using either the complete set of dimensions ("all dimensions" model) or only a subset with sufficient observations by removing low-N dimensions from the input dataset ("high-N only" model). These full models served as reference solutions against which 1.000 bootstrap iterations were compared. We performed a balanced, proportional leave-out bootstrap in which, for each

Appendix B. Results from statistical models comparing older and younger adults in their conceptualization of the four semantic domains.

We report below the results of the ANOVAs and pairwise comparisons conducted on the ordinal regression models we performed, separately for each semantic domain, to compare older and younger adults across all targeted semantic dimensions (see sections 4 and 5.4).

Ecological concepts.

The statistical model yielded a significant interaction between Age Group and Dimensions, X 2 (38) = 1579.4, p < .0001. Pairwise post-hoc comparisons showed that, compared to younger adults, older adults perceive ecological concepts as more linked to contexts (Context Availability, z = 8.569, SE = .105, p < .0001), evoking to a greater extent bodily interactions with their referents (Body-Object Interaction; z = 5.613, SE = .101, p < .0001), more imaginable (Imageability, z = 4.860, SE = .107, p < .0001), easier to define (Easiness of Providing a Definition; z = 4.178, SE = .076, p < .0001), and later acquired (Age of Acquisition, z = 8.872, SE = .098, p < .0001). In addition, older adults conceive ecological concepts as more personally experienced (Personal Experience, z = 10.173, SE = .082, p < .0001) through all bodily parts-feet/legs (z = 8.764, SE = .087, p < .0001), hands/arms (z = 6.216, SE = .086, p < .0001), mouth/throat (z = 15.048, SE = .086, p < .0001), and torso (z = 5.650, SE = .087, p < .0001)-and through vision sensory modality (z = 6.532, SE = .097, p < .0001), as opposed to younger adults who experience them more through senses-in particular, taste (z = 6.161, SE = .120, p < .0001) and touch (z = 5.120, SE = .098, p < .0001).

Additionally, older adults rated ecological concepts as more emotionally charged (Emotionality, z = 6.569, SE = .084, p < .0001) and activating more inner aspects like arousal (Arousal, z = 8.339, SE = .137, p < .0001) and mental processes (Metacognition, z = 2.848, SE = .083, p = .004) than younger adults. For older adults ecological concepts are also more life-impactful, both in the present (Perceived Impact in the Present, z = 14.388, SE = .078, p < .0001), future (Perceived Impact in the Future, z = 16.929, SE = .087, p < .0001), and past (Perceived Impact in the Past, z = 3.433, SE = .078, p < .001). In addition, older adults consider them also more negotiable in their meaning (Openness to Negotiation, z = 5.400, SE = .156, p < .0001), more socially relevant (Social Valence, z = 5.488, SE = .085, p < .0001), and a better starting point for a conversation (Easiness to Start a Conversation, z = 3.405, SE = .136, p < .001). Finally, older adults perceive Age Group Variability Green and Technological Concepts .403, p = .002) and activating less Smell (z = -3.519, SE = .296, p < .001) and Taste (z = -2.552, SE = .508, p = .010) but more the Vision sensory modality (z = 2.759, SE = .099, p = .005).

Instead, no differences emerged between older and younger adults in the activation by technological concepts of the Feet/Legs bodily effectors, in the need both age groups feel to rely on field experts to understand their meaning (Expert Social Metacognition), in technological concepts' Imagineability, in the psychological distance perceived from these concepts (Perceived Distance), and in the degree of personal experiences with them (Personal Experience), and in their Political Relevance, all ps > .082.

Appendix C. Pairwise semantic space age group comparisons across domains.

The following plots illustrate pairwise comparisons across conceptual domains (Ecological, Geo, Natural, and Technological) and show how age-group distinctions emerge in the first principal component (PC1) of each semantic space. Each panel represents the relative distribution of dimensions between two pairs of domains. The colored background quadrants provide a visual reference for the age group polarity of the PC1 loadings: yellow corresponds to dimensions associated with older participants, and light blue to those associated with younger participants. The overlapping areas where the polarity differs between domains are visually emphasized in light green, indicating mismatched regions in the semantic organization of the two spaces. Each point represents a specific dimension, and its color indicates whether its age group classification is consistent across the two domains (green = consistent; red = inconsistent).

On the other hand, younger adults rated to experience natural and geo concepts more through sensory modalities, especially with touch (Geo: z = 12.090, SE = .104, p < .0001; Natural: z =3.537, SE = .099, p < .001) and taste only for geo concepts (z = 7.011, SE = .141, p < .0001).

For both domains, younger adults report more need to rely on both field experts (Expert Social Metacognition, Geo: z = 11.894, SE = .155, p < .0001; Natural: z = 10.257, SE = .151, p < .0001) and generic others (Other Social Metacognition, Geo: z = 6.607, SE = .085, p < .0001; Natural: z = 5.803, SE = .091, p < .0001) to understand their meaning. Regarding only natural concepts, while younger adults perceive that field experts master well their meaning (Confidence in Experts, z = 3.953, SE = .080, p = .0001), older adults instead feel that they master well it (Word Confidence, z = 4.715, SE = .082, p < .0001). In addition, older adults consider natural and geo concepts as more impactful in their past (Perceived Impact in the Past, Geo: z = 2.584, SE = .079, p = .009; Natural: z = 6.169, SE = .080, p < .0001), present (Perceived Impact in the Present, Geo: z = 6.032, SE = .080, p < .0001; Natural: z = 9.473, SE = .079, p < .0001) and future lives (Perceived Impact in the Future, Geo: z = 4.820, SE = .082, p < .0001; Natural: z = 10.869, SE = .081, p < .0001), while younger adults perceive them psychologically farther (Geo: z = 14.547, SE = .101, p < .0001; Natural: z = 17.794, SE = .103, p < .0001).

As for the emotional and inner aspects, older adults conceive both domains as more emotionally loaded than younger adults (Emotionality, Geo: z = 19.689, SE = .083, p < .0001; Natural: z = 12.393, SE = .081, p < .0001) and geo concepts also more positively valences (Valence, z = 2.371, SE = .075, p = .017) and under control (Dominance, z = 5.179, SE = .134, p < .0001). In contrast, younger adults perceive both natural and geo concepts as activating more arousal (Geo: z = 8.943, SE = .138, p < .0001; Natural: z = 4.265, SE = .139, p < .0001) and geo concepts also interoceptive aspects significantly more (Interoception, z = 4.890, SE = .086, p < .0001) than older adults.
